newsitem.title: USA: Conn localities face big unfunded pensions - report.
newsitem.headline: Conn localities face big unfunded pensions - report.

text.p: A Connecticut task force that studied surveys sent in by 130 towns found 13 localities have pensions that are at least 60 percent unfunded, according to an official with the state Office of Policy and Management.

Unfunded pension liabilities are a major concern in Connecticut at the local level, where 65 of its 169 towns faced $1.225 billion of liabilities, according to reports filed with the state through the end of June in 1996.
At the state-level, Connecticut faces a $6 billion to $7 billion problem.

State Treasurer Christopher Burnham has said he opposes selling bonds to finance the unfunded portion of the state's liability, which was expected to be dealt with in part by a new labor pact being negotiated with state workers.

About $500 million of the state's hole has been closed by surging pension investments, and a new bill before the legislature would raise the maximum amount that could be invested in stocks to 65 percent from 55 percent, said Pat O'Neill, a spokesman for Burnham.

Continuing to cut costs in managing the funds also should help narrow the unfunded gap, he added, noting that the number of asset managers has been cut to 30 from around 70 and that all now rely mostly on performance-based pay.

Linda Savitsky, director of municipal services at the state Office of Policy and Management, last Thursday explained that for localities: "We feel that if a plan is funded at 40 percent or less, it is considered as having a problem."

She added the task force expected to complete its work and submit its report to the General Assembly on Tuesday, three days after the deadline set by the bill that created the group to address how to deal with the localities' unfunded pensions.
The group's recommendations were expected to include claifying the law governing whether localities can issue pension obligation bonds, Savitsky said.

While two towns, New Britain and Stratford, had hoped to sell bonds to finance their unfunded pension obligations, both efforts have stalled or died, she said, explaining concerns also have been raised about the legality of such offerings.
"The task force wanted to allow pension obligation bonds, but with state oversight," she said.

Other recommendations were expected to include making a state-wide plan that is available to municipalities more attractive, perhaps by offering more flexible benefits, and having the state treasurer consider creating a voluntary pool to handle towns' investments to cut their administrative costs, though localities would keep fiduciary responsibility.

The cities with some of the biggest problems included Bridgeport, which had a retirement plan for 1,238 police and firefighters that was 100 percent unfunded, with an obligation of over $355 million when the survey was done last autumn, explained Savitsky.

Bridgeport, however, has estimated that its unfunded liability is smaller, at around $250 million to $260 million, and town officials have noted that the city has a fully funded pension pension plan for all police officers who started after 1981, and for all firefighters who joined after 1984. A spokesman for Bridgeport was not immediately available to comment on the state report.

Waterbury had a retirement fund for 3,536 employees that was 82.5 percent unfunded, with an unfunded obligation that totaled $224.5 million, while a New Britain police and firemen's pension fund for 640 employees was 83.6 percent unfunded and had a $113.2 million unfunded obligation, according to Savitsky's data.

Yet the seriousness of the localities' pension problems falls in a broad rang. Some of the unfunded plans, like one for elected officers in North Haven, was 100 percent unfunded but only covers five people with an unfunded obligation of $860,000.

And while Danbury has a pre-1967 pension for 96 employees that was unfunded by 62.7 percent, with an unfunded obligation of $19.4 million, the rest of its retirement programs were overfunded, Savitsky noted.
The other localities with the worst problems were:
--Bridgeport, Janitors and Engineers Retirement Fund, 76 employees, 100 percent unfunded with an unfunded obligation of $9 million.
--Allingtown Fire District Pension Plan, 42 employees, 100 percent unfunded, with a $6.33 million unfunded obligation.
--West Shore, Retirement Plan for Employees of West Shore Fire District, 54 employees, 97.2 percent unfunded, with an unfunded obligation of $14.7 million.
--First Fire District Pension Fund, 106 employees, 96.6 percent unfunded, with an unfunded pension obligation of $23.7 million.
--City of West Haven Police Pension Fund, 208 employees, 87 percent unfunded, with an unfunded pension liability of $45.9 million.
--Town of Stratford Employees Retirement Plan, 826 employees, 76.6 percent unfunded, with an unfunded liability of $81.2 million.
--Naugatuck, Borough Employees Pension Plan, 734 employees, 70.7 percent unfunded, with an unfunded pension liability of $34.1 million.
--The Town of Deep River Employees Retirement Plan and Trust, 28 employees, 70.3 percent unfunded, with an unfunded liability of $248,000.
